591.event_title: Babur loses his homeland and goes on to found the Mughal Empire
591.place: Fergana and Samarkand (Central Asia), Kabul, and Panipat, India
591.event: Babur inherited the kingdom of Fergana as a boy in 1494 and spent years trying to hold Samarkand, but in the end lost both Samarkand and his native Fergana. He took Kabul in 1504 and made it his base, and after several raids into India he defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi of Delhi at the First Battle of Panipat in April 1526. By his death in 1530 he had laid the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
591.explanation: Having lost every possession he was born to, Babur still had the drive that let him build something far larger than what he lost.
591.tie_back: The kural says the only real possession is inner energy and that those without it do not truly own even what they hold, and Babur's life shows energy outlasting the loss of a whole kingdom.
591._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of energy as the possession that survives the loss of all others; the kural is about inner drive, while Babur's story is also one of military conquest.

592.event_title: Thomas Carlyle rewrites The French Revolution after the only manuscript is burned
592.event: After spending months in 1834 on the first volume of his history of the French Revolution, Thomas Carlyle lent his only draft to the philosopher John Stuart Mill, in whose house it was accidentally burned. When Mill confessed, Carlyle responded generously and began to reconstruct the work at once. The completed three-volume The French Revolution was published in 1837 and established his reputation; a small burnt fragment is kept at Carlyle's House in Chelsea.
592.explanation: What Carlyle owned, a finished manuscript, vanished overnight, but the power of mind that had produced it remained and produced it again.
592.tie_back: The kural says energy of mind is the possession that lasts while other possessions slip away, and Carlyle's lost manuscript and rewritten book are a vivid example.
592._accuracy_note: Closely matches the contrast between a possession that departs and inner energy that stays; the possession lost here is a manuscript rather than money.

593.event_title: Thomas Edison rebuilds after the West Orange factory fire
593.place: West Orange, New Jersey, United States
593.event: In December 1914 a fire destroyed much of the factory complex surrounding Thomas Edison's laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey, although the laboratory buildings themselves survived. The loss was very large, but Edison led the rebuilding of the works. He continued his business and research there through the First World War, during which he also chaired the Naval Consulting Board.
593.explanation: Edison treated the destruction of a great part of his property as a setback to be repaired rather than a disaster to be mourned.
593.tie_back: The kural says those who firmly hold energy do not grieve over lost wealth, and Edison's response to the fire was to rebuild rather than lament.
593._accuracy_note: A strong fit for not grieving over lost wealth; famous quotations attributed to Edison about the fire are not included because they could not be verified.

594.event_title: Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita found the company that became Sony
594.event: In 1946, in a Tokyo still recovering from the war, Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo (Tokyo Telecommunications Engineering Corporation), which began by making devices such as voltmeters. Early consumer products, including an electric rice cooker and Japan's first tape recorder, sold poorly, but the founders licensed the transistor from Bell Laboratories in the early 1950s and built transistor radios. The company renamed itself Sony in 1958 and in 1961 became the first Japanese company to list its shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
594.explanation: Two engineers with little capital kept working through failures, and prosperity followed their persistence rather than preceding it.
594.tie_back: The kural says prosperity finds its own way to the home of the person whose energy never wavers, and Sony's growth from a small postwar workshop shows it arriving after years of steady effort.
594._accuracy_note: A reasonable fit for prosperity following persistent effort; success also depended on technology licensing and market conditions, not energy alone.

595.event_title: Wilma Rudolph overcomes childhood polio to win three Olympic golds
595.event: Wilma Rudolph, born in Tennessee in 1940, contracted polio and other illnesses as a child and for years could not walk without a leg brace or special shoe. With years of treatment and exercise she learned to walk normally and became a sprinter. At the 1960 Rome Olympics she won gold in the 100 metres, the 200 metres and the 4 x 100 metres relay, becoming the first American woman to win three track and field gold medals at a single Games.
595.explanation: Rudolph's rise was not set by the body she started with but by the strength of her will and effort.
595.tie_back: The kural says a person rises as high as the energy of their mind, just as a lotus stalk grows as tall as the water is deep, and Rudolph rose from a leg brace to the top of the Olympic podium.
595._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of height achieved in proportion to inner energy; sources differ on the age at which she stopped needing the brace.

596.event_title: Scott's party reaches the South Pole and dies on the return
596.place: South Pole and the Ross Ice Shelf, Antarctica
596.event: Captain Robert Falcon Scott led the British Antarctic (Terra Nova) Expedition, whose five-man polar party reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912, only to find that Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party had arrived there on 14 December 1911. All five men died on the return journey, Scott himself with Edward Wilson and Henry Bowers in late March, held up by a blizzard about 11 miles from a supply depot. A search party found their tent, bodies, diaries and photographs the following November.
596.explanation: Scott's party aimed at one of the hardest goals of their age and reached it, but fate denied them both priority and survival; they are still remembered for the height of their aim and their endurance.
596.tie_back: The kural urges people to let every thought be of rising higher, and says that even if fate thwarts that aim, it keeps the worth of not having been thwarted, which is how Scott's expedition has been remembered.
596._accuracy_note: Fits the idea of a lofty aim defeated by fate yet retaining its honour; the expedition's planning decisions are still debated by historians.

597.event_title: Rana Pratap fights on after the defeat at Haldighati
597.event: In June 1576 Rana Pratap Singh of Mewar was defeated by a Mughal army of the emperor Akbar at the Battle of Haldighati near Gogunda. Instead of submitting, he withdrew to the hills and continued resistance from mountain strongholds, later making Chavand his capital. He kept raiding until his death in 1597, and Mewar did not formally acknowledge Mughal overlordship until 1614.
597.explanation: Defeat in open battle did not break Pratap's resolve, and he spent the rest of his life standing his ground in the hills.
597.tie_back: The kural says the strong-minded do not falter even in ruin, like a war elephant that stands firm though pierced by arrows, and Pratap held firm for two decades after Haldighati.
597._accuracy_note: A close match to steadfastness in ruin; popular legends about Pratap are excluded, and only the basic course of his resistance is given.

598.event_title: Milton Hershey rises from bankruptcy to found a school for orphaned boys
598.place: Philadelphia, New York and Hershey, Pennsylvania, United States
598.event: Milton Hershey's first candy business in Philadelphia went bankrupt after six years, and a second attempt in New York also failed. Returning to Lancaster with little money, he built the Lancaster Caramel Company, sold it in 1900 for one million dollars, and went on to build the Hershey Chocolate Company. On 15 November 1909 he and his wife Catherine signed the deed of trust founding the Hershey Industrial School for orphaned boys, and in 1918 he placed his controlling interest in the chocolate company in trust for the school.
598.explanation: The same drive that carried Hershey through repeated business failures later made him one of the most generous benefactors of his time.
598.tie_back: The kural says those without energy of spirit will never know the proud joy of being generous givers, and Hershey's school shows the giving that energy made possible.
598._accuracy_note: Fits the chain from energy to wealth to generosity that commentators read in the kural; the kural speaks of the pride of a giver, which the sources do not describe in Hershey's own words.

599.event_title: The Athenians defeat the Persian army at Marathon
599.event: In 490 BCE a Persian expeditionary force sent by King Darius I landed at the bay of Marathon, northeast of Athens. About 10,000 Athenians and 1,000 Plataeans, without Spartan help, faced a larger Persian army and, under generals including Miltiades, attacked with a thinned centre and strengthened wings that routed the Persian flanks and then closed on the centre. The Persians withdrew to their ships and sailed away.
599.explanation: The smaller force won because of its boldness and determination, not its numbers.
599.tie_back: The kural says that the huge, sharp-tusked elephant still takes fright when a tiger attacks, meaning that spirit and energy defeat sheer size, as the Athenians showed at Marathon.
599._accuracy_note: A classic case of a smaller, bolder force defeating a larger one; the size of the Persian army is uncertain, and tactics as well as spirit decided the battle.

600.event_title: The deaf Beethoven completes and premieres his Ninth Symphony
600.event: Ludwig van Beethoven's hearing had been failing since his late twenties, and by the 1820s he was profoundly deaf. He nevertheless completed his Ninth Symphony, with a choral finale setting Schiller's Ode to Joy, and it was first performed at the Theater am Karntnertor in Vienna on 7 May 1824. Beethoven stood on stage beside the conductor indicating the tempos while the performance was actually directed by others.
600.explanation: Deprived of the sense on which a composer most depends, Beethoven still produced one of the most celebrated works in Western music.
600.tie_back: The kural says a person's real strength is abundance of inner energy, and Beethoven's Ninth shows that energy accomplishing what physical loss seemed to forbid.
600._accuracy_note: A strong example of inner strength overcoming physical limits; the kural's harsh contrast with people who are no better than trees is not illustrated.
